author: Al Jazeera English
description:
More than three years into Israel's war on Gaza, displaced Palestinian families continue to live in overcrowded makeshift tents, struggling with a lack of basic hygiene facilities, cooking supplies and adequate protection from the elements. In Deir el-Balah, central Gaza, a family of seven shares a cramped tent with little privacy, relying on scraps of wood and other materials to cook amid shortages of fuel and essential supplies. Displaced residents say mattresses have worn out, hygiene products are scarce and the tents offer little protection from winter cold, summer heat, mosquitoes or rodents. Despite the ceasefire, Palestinians say restrictions on the entry of humanitarian supplies and prefabricated housing units are preventing them from moving beyond temporary shelter. As winter sets in, families fear conditions will deteriorate further, with many still waiting for the chance to return home or rebuild their lives. 

Al Jazeera's Tareq Abu Azzoum reports from Deir el-Balah, Gaza.
title: Gaza’s displaced families remain trapped in makeshift shelters three years on

description:
Leaders and their political parties across Africa are extending term limits; not by coup, but by democratic process: changing the constitution by vote or referendum. 

Ahmed Idris in Abuja, Nigeria tells us about the history and process of changing constitutions. 

Haru Mutasa focuses on Zimbabwe, where this summer, a new law extended President Emmerson Mnangagwa's term. 

Chris Ocamringa takes us through an ongoing political process in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where a new law is leading to a referendum that could extend the president's term.

description:
A youth-led movement born as online satire has unsettled Indian politics. Named after a dismissive remark by the chief justice, the Cockroach Janta Party has mobilised some of the country’s biggest protests in years. They have been driven by anger over exam leaks, unemployment and a lack of political accountability.

The demonstrators have been met by heavy police crackdowns and clashed with mainstream media outlets they accuse of serving the government.

As young Indians turn to social media and independent outlets to tell their stories, this film examines the growing divide between India’s youth and mainstream media and what it could mean for the future of politics and journalism.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
For more than a million Rohingya refugees, Cox’s Bazar was meant to be a place of safety. Instead, it has become a life on hold. Filmed entirely inside the camps in Bangladesh, this film follows six people: a widowed mother newly arrived from Myanmar, a father supporting his family through a small betel-leaf business, a student and advocate, an artist, a musician and a young man forced to conceal his identity for protection. Together, they face shrinking food aid, restricted opportunities, separation from loved ones and no clear route home. The Islamic holy month of Ramadan forms the backdrop, bringing moments of faith, family and communal ritual into sharper relief amid mounting hardship. Made with a Rohingya producer and director of photography living in the settlement, the film offers an intimate view from within: people working, studying, creating and caring for their families while fighting to preserve their dignity.

The challenges posed by antimicrobial resistance show where its impact is most acutely and tragically manifested: infant mortality in the developing world, specifically in sub-Saharan Africa. This film shows what these bland statistics mean in real terms to the health workers and families affected, following them as they struggle to fight this battle with low-tech solutions.

The Drugs Don’t Work follows the battle to the United Kingdom and examines how and why penicillin, the world’s most successful antibiotic, was invented. It then examines why pharmaceutical companies like GlaxoSmithKline are struggling to produce novel solutions to the problem of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

The film also explores the cutting edge of academic research at British universities and hospitals supported by the power of the UK-based tech company DeepMind, and features academics and advocates who are devoting their lives to solving the problem. This week: 408 days after the declaration of a ceasefire in Gaza,  Israel has killed at least 1,658 Palestinians there.  Israel carried out its first significant ground operation in Gaza since the ceasefire. Parents in Gaza are improvising to entertain their children. Israel has killed at least 74,710 Palestinians in Gaza since October 7, 2023.

In this episode:

- Hind Khoudary, Al Jazeera Correspondent  
- Ibrhaim Al-Khalili, Al Jazeera Correspondent

Episode credits:

This episode was produced and mixed by David Enders. Our sound designer is Alex Roldan. Adam Abou-Gad is our engagement producer. Alexandra Locke is The Take’s executive producer.
title: Brief: Israel's launches first ground operation in Gaza since ceasefire | The Take

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
The UK Foreign Secretary says rejoining the European Union could be on the table once talks resume in Brussels. Ed Miliband's comments come after Prime Minister Andy Burnham struck a deal with EU leaders to reset relations, a decade after Brexit.

Al Jazeera's Milena Veselinovic says the deals could open a path back to EU membership after the next UK election. She says Burnham is known to want Britain back in the EU, but insists he will not pursue it before the next general election, scheduled for 2029.

Veselinovic says disappointment with Brexit does not automatically mean support for rejoining.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, one of the architects of Brexit, says Burnham has no mandate for the changes because he has not won a general election.

Al Jazeera's Milena Veselinovic reports from London.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian says his country is facing a "silent economic war" that is even tougher than a military conflict involving missiles. 

Al Jazeera's Resul Serdar says the Iranian armed forces say 25 vessels have hit sea mines since last Saturday. He says Iranians believe the US is imposing a total economic war through the naval blockade, and that Tehran considers escalation less costly than the blockade becoming permanent.

Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, says Trump has not yet decided whether to escalate. He says that if Trump does not, he may declare victory and walk away, but would need to soften the blockade and some sanctions, because continuing it will bring escalation. Parsi says Iran's missile display is meant to deter a US strike.

Al Jazeera's Resul Serdar reports from Tehran.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Days of heavy rainfall in Florida have flooded communities along its Atlantic coast. People have been told to prepare to leave the area, with water levels expected to rise in the coming week.

Thousands of homes are submerged and inaccessible except by airboat. Florida National Guard troops are rescuing people along the state's east coast. 

Some families say they had just minutes to escape the rising waters. One woman says her car was underwater and she had to get her son out. Another says everything she owned is destroyed.

The governor has declared a state of emergency in 21 counties. Officials say the rain is easing, but floodwaters are still rising. 

Al Jazeera's Ama Boateng reports.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Residents of the English village of Barnham have voted to leave the United Kingdom in an unofficial, symbolic referendum. The vote is in protest against government plans to turn a nearby military site into asylum accommodation for more than 900 people.

Helen Beck, chair of the Barnham Residents Association, says leaving the UK is not technically on the table, and that the vote is an attempt to get local voices heard. She says residents feel nobody is listening to their concerns.

Local business owner Steph Donaldson says services are already struggling. Charity Suffolk Refugee Support warns that people in large, isolated centres can suffer stress and isolation.

The Home Office says it recognises the strength of feeling in local communities and is listening carefully to concerns.

Al Jazeera's Camille Nedelec reports from Barnham, Suffolk.
